638.title: Rama's vow of refuge
638.hook: the enemy's brother asks to be let in; the camp argues; Rama vows refuge to anyone who comes
638.carry: sharanagati: whoever comes once is held
638.howItsDone: In the Sri Vaishnava tradition the Vibhishana episode is taught as the model of śaraṇāgati, taking refuge, and Rama's vow in Yuddha Kanda 18 is recited and commented on as a central verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vibhishana's crossing. He told Ravana the truth, was called a disgrace, and crossed the sea. Sharanagati: I've come to Rama for refuge.

A war camp on a beach, the eve of battle. A figure appears in the sky above it, with four armed companions, and calls down: I'm the enemy king's brother, please let me in. Sugriva, king of the monkeys, doesn't hesitate. He goes straight to Rama: this is a trick. He's a rakshasa, Ravana's own brother, and he'll strike when we're not looking. Kill him, or send him away. The whole camp starts arguing.
screen: `A FIGURE IN THE SKY.` → `THIS IS A TRICK.` → `THE CAMP ARGUES.`

segments.voice: Rama asks his council, and Valmiki lets every voice speak. Angada says test him first. Others say send a spy, or question him closely. Then Hanuman speaks, the one who has actually been inside Lanka. He came openly, not in disguise. I've watched his face, and I see no deceit in it. Accept him. Then Rama gives his answer. I can't turn away someone who comes as a friend, even if he has faults. And then something larger. Anyone who comes to me even once and says, I am yours, I give safety from every being. That is my vow. Sugriva still pushes back. Rama goes further. Even if it were Ravana himself, bring him in. In the Sri Vaishnava tradition of South India, this verse is treasured as a teaching on sharanagati, taking refuge in God: the one who turns to God even once, sincerely, is held. Others read it more plainly, as the code of a good king toward someone asking for protection. Then Rama has Vibhishana come down, sends for sea water, and pours it over his head, consecrating him king of Lanka, right there on the beach, before a single battle has been fought. That vow is why so many Hindus aren't afraid to come back to the shrine after years away: by Rama's own word, one sincere turning is enough. And Sugriva's question is still asked today, at lunch tables and family dinners, whenever someone who hurt us asks to come back: what if it's a trick? Rama never calls the caution foolish. He just says the refuge is bigger.

639.title: Rama spares the spies
639.hook: two spies dressed as monkeys are caught in Rama's camp, and he lets them go unharmed
639.carry: maryada: dharma keeps its limits in war
639.howItsDone: Storytellers often use the release of Shuka and Sarana to show the code of war in the Ramayana: an unarmed messenger or captive is not killed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vibhishana's crossing. Rama vowed safety to anyone who comes even once and says I am yours, and crowned Vibhishana on the beach. Sharanagati: whoever comes once is held.

The army crosses the bridge and spreads out along Lanka's shore. Across the island, Ravana does what any general would. He sends two of his ministers, Shuka and Sarana, to count the enemy. They take the shape of monkeys and slip in among the troops. It almost works. But one person in that camp knows exactly what a rakshasa in disguise looks like, because he grew up among them. Vibhishana sees through them, and they're dragged before Rama.
screen: `THE ARMY IS ACROSS.` → `TWO SPIES DRESSED AS MONKEYS.` → `VIBHISHANA SEES THROUGH THEM.`

segments.voice: In a war story, you know what usually happens to caught spies, and the monkeys are ready to do it. The two rakshasas, terrified, confess: Ravana sent us to count your army. And Rama laughs. If you've seen everything, he says, go back. If you missed anything, look again; Vibhishana will show you around. You're unarmed and you were caught. You won't be killed. Then he hands them a message for Ravana: show me the strength you relied on when you carried Sita away. The spies go home, name Rama's leaders one by one from Ravana's tower, and end with advice he doesn't want: make peace and return Sita. Ravana throws them out. Hindus have a name for Rama that this scene shows: maryada purushottam, the best of men, who keeps the bounds of dharma. Maryada means a boundary. Rama has every reason to be cruel here: it's war, his wife is a captive, the enemy is spying on him. And still there's a line he won't cross. Hindu teaching calls this dharma yuddha, righteous war, and the Mahabharata sets out such rules before its own great battle: you don't strike the unarmed, or someone who can't fight back. Rama isn't soft. His message is a hard one. But winning doesn't move the line. Today, the spies are more likely to be screenshots. When you've caught someone in the wrong and could make an example of them, maryada asks one question: is this something a person of dharma does, even when they could?

640.title: One last offer of peace
640.hook: Lanka surrounded at four gates, and still Rama sends Angada with an offer of peace
640.howItsDone: In North Indian Ramlila performances, Angada's embassy to Ravana's court is a well-known scene, often played in the Ramcharitmanas version with Angada's unmovable foot.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the siege began with two spies caught and sent home unharmed. Even in war, Rama keeps dharma's limits. Maryada.

Rama climbs Mount Suvela with his leaders to look at Lanka. And there, on a high tower across the way, stands Ravana himself, in royal clothes, among his attendants. Sugriva can't stand it. Without a word to anyone he leaps across, lands on the tower, knocks off Ravana's crown, and the two kings wrestle. Then Sugriva jumps back, pleased with himself. Rama is not pleased. A king doesn't do that, he says. If something had happened to you, what would I have done?
screen: `RAVANA ON HIS TOWER.` → `SUGRIVA LEAPS ACROSS.` → `A KING DOESN'T DO THAT.`

segments.voice: Then Rama does things in order. Lanka has four great gates, and he assigns a leader to each: Nila to the east, Angada to the south, Hanuman to the west, and Rama himself, with Lakshmana, to the north, where Ravana is. The city is surrounded. And still, before the first blow, Rama sends a messenger: Angada, Vali's son. Angada leaps to Ravana's palace and speaks plainly: return Sita, ask pardon, and you'll live. If not, Vibhishana will rule Lanka. Ravana orders him seized. Four rakshasas grab him by the arms. Angada springs onto the palace roof with all four hanging on; they drop off, he breaks the roof's peak, and leaps back to Rama. You may know a later scene from Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, Angada's foot planted in Ravana's court that no one can lift. In Valmiki it's the broken rooftop. Here's the teaching underneath. Old Hindu teaching on kingship names four ways to settle a conflict: sama, talking and making peace; dana, giving; bheda, splitting the other side; and danda, force. Force comes last. Hanuman weighs all four in Lanka before he fights, and the Mahabharata shows it on a bigger stage: before Kurukshetra, Krishna himself goes to the Kauravas' court to ask for peace. So Rama, with every gate covered, still starts with sama. Only after Angada returns does the battle begin. Today, most sieges are smaller: a family feud, a friend group split in two. Sama first means the plain offer of peace comes before anything else, even when you could win.

641.title: Even Rama falls
641.hook: arrows from an empty sky, and Rama, God on earth, falls like a man
641.carry: the avatar lives a real human life
641.howItsDone: Ramayana tellers often slow down at the serpent-arrows, the nāgapāśa, letting listeners sit with the heroes' fall before the rescue comes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the siege. Lanka surrounded, and still Angada carried one last offer before the battle began. Sama first: peace before force.

The first day of fighting goes badly for Lanka. Duel after duel, the monkey and bear leaders win, and the rakshasa champions fall or run. The sun sets, and the fighting goes on in the dark, by the light of weapons. In one duel, Angada smashes the chariot of Ravana's son, killing his horses and driver. The prince jumps clear. Then he does something the monkeys have no answer for. He disappears.
screen: `A GOOD FIRST DAY.` → `FIGHTING IN THE DARK.` → `HE DISAPPEARS.`

segments.voice: His name is Indrajit, conqueror of Indra, king of the gods; the epic says he once carried Indra off as a captive. Now he rises out of sight among the clouds and starts shooting. Valmiki says the arrows turn into serpents as they strike, wrapping Rama and Lakshmana tight, until the two brothers can't move. They fall side by side, covered in shafts. Sugriva, Hanuman and Jambavan gather around them, stunned. Indrajit shouts down that they're dead, and goes home to tell his father. Stop on that picture, because it's strange. For Hindus, Rama is Vishnu himself, come down to earth. That's what avatar means: a descent. So how can God lie bound on a battlefield? The story's answer, as Hindus hear it, is that the descent is real. Rama doesn't pretend to be human; he lives it. At the very end of the war, when the gods come to praise him, Rama says: I think of myself as a man, Rama, son of Dasharatha. Many Hindu teachers read that as the heart of the avatar: God doesn't watch a human life from above, he goes all the way in, fear, grief and defeat included. And Valmiki doesn't rush to the rescue. The first night of the war ends with the heroes down, the sky quiet, and nobody sure whether they're alive. That's why a Hindu can pray to Rama on the worst night of a hard year. He has lain on that field. A fall doesn't mean God has gone; in this story, God is the one lying there.

642.title: Trijata's comfort
642.hook: Ravana flies Sita over the battlefield to break her, and a rakshasi from his own house reads the signs

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indrajit's arrows brought Rama and Lakshmana down. The avatar lives a real human life, falls included.

Indrajit reports to his father: they're dead. Ravana is delighted, and he thinks of Sita. If she sees them lying there, she'll stop hoping, and she'll be his. So he has her put in the Pushpaka, the flying chariot, and flown out over the battlefield. Below her, among the shattered monkey army, she sees them: Rama and Lakshmana on the ground, bound and still, pierced all over with arrows. And she breaks down.
screen: `THEY'RE DEAD, FATHER.` → `SITA FLOWN OVER THE FIELD.` → `SHE BREAKS DOWN.`

segments.voice: Sita's lament in Valmiki is raw. She recalls the signs read on her body as a girl, promising she'd never be a widow, and calls them all lies. Beside her in the chariot is Trijata, a rakshasi, one of her guards from the ashoka grove, who had dreamed of Ravana's fall and told the others to leave Sita alone. Her comfort now is careful, almost like evidence in a trial. Look at their faces, she says. The faces of the dead lose their color; theirs haven't. Look at the army: if the leader were dead, they'd be scattered and running. Instead they're gathered around him, guarding him. And the last sign: this Pushpaka would not carry you if you were a widow. They're alive. So Sita is flown back to the grove, still afraid, but holding on. Down on the field, Rama wakes first. The serpents still hold him, but his grief is all for his brother, and he tells Sugriva to take the army home. Now look at who is good in this war, and who isn't. Ravana is the grandson of a great sage, Pulastya, and learned in the Vedas. The ones choosing truth and kindness are Vibhishana, who crossed the sea, and Trijata, a rakshasi from Ravana's own household, beside a weeping prisoner. Many teachers read the Ramayana this way: dharma isn't something you're born into; it's what you choose to do. Ravana sent Sita up to lose hope, and someone from his own house sent her down with some. Worth remembering at school or at work, when someone from the other side is the one who tells you the truth, kindly.

643.title: Garuda comes for Rama
643.hook: a great wind over the battlefield, the snakes let go, and Vishnu's own eagle comes for Rama
643.carry: rama is vishnu, and garuda knows
643.howItsDone: In recitations of the Yuddha Kanda, the Garuda episode comes straight after the brothers' fall, and tellers often slow down at Garuda's refusal to say why he came.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Trijata, a rakshasi from Ravana's own house, read the signs and held Sita up. Dharma lives in deeds, not in birth.

Night on the battlefield, and the camp is out of ideas. Rama lies bound beside his brother. Sugriva wants to carry them home. Sushena, the monkey physician, says there are healing herbs on mountains far off in the ocean of milk, and someone should be sent. While they're still talking, the wind changes. A great wind comes off the sea. Clouds tear open, the waves heave, the hills shake, and trees on the shore bend flat. Something enormous is coming down out of the sky.
screen: `OUT OF IDEAS.` → `A GREAT WIND OFF THE SEA.` → `SOMETHING COMING DOWN.`

segments.voice: It's Garuda: the great eagle, king of the birds, blazing like fire. The moment the serpents feel him coming, they let go. The arrows that were snakes slither off the brothers and flee; in the old stories, serpents and Garuda are enemies. Garuda bows to the brothers and strokes their faces with his hands, and Valmiki says their wounds close at once, and they rise brighter and stronger than before. Rama, amazed, asks: who are you? The answer is warm, and mysterious. I'm your friend, Garutman, he says, like your own breath moving outside your body. Then, just when you'd expect him to say why he's come, he doesn't. Don't ask, he says, more or less. You'll understand when the battle is over. He walks around Rama in a circle of respect, and flies off. The monkey army sees the brothers standing and roars so loud that Ravana hears it inside his palace. So why would Garuda come, and why the secret? In Hindu tradition, Garuda is the eagle Vishnu rides. And his promise comes true: when the war is over, Valmiki has Brahma himself tell Rama who he is: Narayana, Vishnu. Hindus hear the whole Ramayana with both sides at once: a real man in a real war, who never claims to be God, and Vishnu on earth, whose own eagle comes down when he falls. If a friend ever asks a Hindu kid whether Rama is a hero or a god, this is the answer: both. And this is the scene that shows it.

644.title: Why Garuda carries Vishnu
644.hook: why the snakes run from Garuda, and why the strongest bird faces Vishnu with folded hands
644.carry: vahana: garuda's strength bows to vishnu
644.howItsDone: Garuda's story from the Mahabharata's Adi Parva is often told to children, and in many Vishnu temples a figure of Garuda faces the main shrine with folded hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Garuda came down in a great wind, freed the brothers, and wouldn't say why. Rama is Vishnu, and Garuda knows.

The arrows that were snakes didn't fight Garuda. The moment his wind reached the shore, they fled. People who grew up with Indian tales know why. They've heard it from grandparents, in comics, in temple carvings. It's a story about two sisters, a horse's tail, a cheat, and a son who will do anything to set his mother free. Valmiki doesn't stop to tell it, so here it is.
screen: `THE SNAKES DON'T FIGHT. THEY FLEE.` → `TWO SISTERS AND A HORSE'S TAIL.` → `A SON WHO FREES HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: It's told in the Mahabharata's first book. Two sisters, Kadru and Vinata, are both wives of the sage Kashyapa. Kadru is the mother of the serpents; Vinata is the mother of Garuda. The sisters bet on the color of a divine horse's tail, and the loser becomes the winner's servant. Kadru cheats: she has her serpent sons hang on the tail so it looks black. Vinata loses, and becomes a servant to her sister and the snakes. Her son Garuda asks the serpents what it will take to free his mother. Bring us the nectar of immortality, they say, from the gods. So Garuda storms heaven and wins the nectar, and he doesn't taste a drop himself. On the way, Vishnu, pleased with him, offers him a gift, and Garuda in turn agrees to serve Vishnu, as the bird he rides and the emblem on his banner. He frees his mother. That's why snakes and Garuda are enemies, and why Garuda carries Vishnu. Every Hindu god has a vahana, a mount: Shiva's bull Nandi, Ganesha's mouse, Durga's lion. Garuda is Vishnu's. That's why, in many Vishnu temples, a figure of Garuda faces the main shrine with folded hands, the way a devotee does. Think what that shows: the bird who stormed heaven for his mother, strong enough to scatter serpents at Lanka, kept forever in service, hands joined. Many teachers read the vahana that way: the greatest strength bows. So when you see Garuda in a temple, or in a family shrine, you're looking at a picture of what strength is for.
